  • Cooling score (0..100, higher is better): 70% temperature rise over ambient (under high load) + 30% total fan RPM (under high load). Inside the temperature term: CPU 40 points, GPU 30 points, VRM 10 points (CPU outweighs GPU by 10, VRM is the tiebreaker). Anchors: 0 C adjusted rise → 100, 40 C → 0; 0 RPM → 100, 8000 RPM → 0.
  • Workload-intensity compensation: the score forgives up to 10 C of extra hotspot rise proportional to the workload intensity (clocks, voltages, power under load). A pegged-out system is genuinely producing more heat — that's not the airflow's fault — so it gets a credit. An idle/light run gets no credit and its temps must speak for themselves.
  • Workload intensity (0..100): mean of CPU and GPU sub-scores. Each sub-score averages clock, voltage and power scaled against typical desktop maxima (CPU: 5.0 GHz, 0.9–1.4 V, 150 W; GPU: 3.0 GHz, 0.7–1.1 V, 350 W). 100 means the silicon was running flat out during the load samples.
  • Rise over ambient (C): hotspot median minus the motherboard "System" sensor. Cancels out room-temperature differences between sessions.
  • Cooling efficiency (C/W): rise over ambient divided by that component's median power draw while loaded. Lower = the cooler removes more heat per watt produced.
  • High load: samples where CPU load ≥ 10% or GPU load ≥ 30%. The CPU gate is intentionally low because a powerful CPU heats up even at light loads; the GPU gate is higher because GPUs stay cool until they're actively rendering.
  • Headroom to throttle (C): distance from the 95th percentile temperature to the throttling threshold (CPU 95 C, GPU hot spot 90 C, VRM 100 C). Bigger = safer.

Correlation heatmap (Spearman, |r| ≥ 0.3)

Black cells mark |r| = 1: the diagonal (trivially self-correlated) plus any off-diagonal pair that carries no extra information beyond the other. Note: raw correlation between fan RPM and temperature can be misleading because fans ramp up when temperatures rise — see the Fan Impact Matrix below for a controlled answer to "which fan cools which sensor".

Fan Impact Matrix — which fan cools which sensor

Each cell is the change in that temperature (in °C) per +1000 RPM of that fan, after controlling for CPU load, GPU load, CPU package power, GPU package power, ambient (System sensor), and every other fan in the case. Restricted to warm samples (CPU load ≥ 10% or GPU load ≥ 30%). Negative (blue) = cooling. More negative is better. Cells with a hatch pattern have low tolerance (this fan moves nearly identically to another fan in the data, so its individual effect can't be separated reliably; the sign is OK but the magnitude isn't).
